I have wanted to be a wife and mother my whole life, against the wishes of my family, teachers, and pretty much every leader I've ever had. I was encouraged from all angles to find a career, but there was just nothing outside of homemaking that interested me. I actively started seeking a husband as soon as I turned 18, but I've never been pretty and men for the most are just not attracted to me. As I approached 30 unmarried and with no prospects, I started realizing I would need to find a way to support myself. Through a series of events, I was able to find a career that I became very passionate about. I went to college to get a degree, and began working in my field. Although I was unmarried, I was still very happy with my life (I've always been a naturally content person). I absolutely loved my job, my coworkers, my community, where I lived.

Then, I met the man who is now my husband, got married, and moved away to the city where he is stationed in the military. And now, having achieved my lifelong dream, I'm unfulfilled, unhappy, and terribly lonely. I'm pregnant and dreading having a child. I'm not excited about it at all, which has been shocking for me. I miss my career and my old life. I love my husband so much and he is the best husband I could have possibly hoped for and I know I'm fortunate to have him. And don't get me wrong - nothing is wrong in my life. Everything has worked out the way I always wanted it to. The thing is, it just doesn't feel like I thought it would. I feel so empty. And I feel terribly ashamed for even feeling this way, because I am being selfish and ungrateful and because I am the manifestation of what I always thought was a feminist lie: that housewives are trapped and miserable. But that's why I'm posting here, in the hopes that maybe someone can offer advice. I would never even consider leaving my husband or anything like that. I made a commitment, and I will keep it no matter what. But I cry almost every day and I keep wondering - will I feel like this forever? How do I cope?

It's not always exactly like that. It is for many women, and that's fantastic, but I just want to share my experience and thoughts in case it isn't love at first sight for you.

I truly believed I would fall in love with my baby the second I saw her. Maybe in part due to my birth experience, I didn't love her at first.

I was with it enough to be logically protective of my baby. The doctors and midwives wanted to cut the cord straight away and rub her vigoursly, I brushed them off and I told them we are waiting at least 5 minutes to cut the cord. They had a huge clock (a bit bigger than one foot tall digital numbers, and only about two metres away) counting up the minutes and seconds since my baby was born. I kept looking at the clock and did not get to bond properly until we got out of the hospital nearly a week later (nothing really wrong with us, they were just paranoid due to birth circumstances).

Breastfeeding helped once I got the hang of it. Staring at her (awake or asleep) helped. Kissing her helped... honestly I was only doing it at first because it changes breastmilk to benefit the baby's immune system: customises it to the germs on baby's skin etc. I also licked her as well!

Being attentive to my baby's needs and consciously being a good mother helped a lot. It was a blur but slowly I fell in love.

Also pregnancy hormones are bitch. Also beware of the baby blues in the first week when your milk comes in. It was also really hard for me believe I was pregnant or even a mother until we had bonded a bit after she was born.

Hang in there! It will be amazing. Just trust yourself. You won't feel like this forever.

That slowly changes with time. Mine are teens now and even though we homeschool I have a lot more time for my own interests and hobbies again...I think I have more hobbies now than before I had kids. It feels like they'll be little forever and then one day your baby boy has beard hairs on his chin and stands a few inches taller than you, and you wonder where the years went.

The grass is always greener on the other side. And happiness is not a destination at which you can arrive, or a place in which you can live. Sometimes in life you will feel happy, but it's not ever going to be permanent. That's not how life works. If we make it our goal we will inevitably be disappointed. We all do that...we make a plan and assume that once we succeed in reaching our goal, we'll be happy and everything will be perfect. And it never is. It's like fat people who think that all their body insecurities will go away once they lose the weight, only to find that they still don't feel good enough. Your life didn't go the way you expected; you wanted to marry young and it didn't happen. You wanted to be a homemaker but a girl's gotta eat so you got into a career and learned to love it. You married and moved and thought you'd be happy and now you're not. I promise you, this happens to all of us in one way or another - our dreams of what life will look like are often so different from what life actually looks like. When I was young, I imagined a future where we had an old rambling house bursting with children...instead I miscarried three early babies, had a full-term stillbirth, and almost lost the two kids who did survive while I was pregnant with them. There is always going to be a hole in this family where another kid should have been. I envisioned a future where my husband and i shared our faith together and taught our six children Bible stories around the fireplace in the evenings; instead, my husband deconverted and spent almost a decade as an atheist before eventually finding his way back to a different kind of faith. I thought I was gonna be such a great wife, but then I found myself making some horrible choices that put my marriage in danger, and I had to face the fact that I am capable of being a terrible person and justifying it. Life doesn't do what we think it will. And it hurts. It's disappointing. It's hard. It's humbling. And then there are the expectations we place on how things will feel. For many years, Christmas was sad for me because I kept trying to recapture the magic of my childhood memories and recreate those feelings - I was sure that if I just did all the same baking, decorated my tree the same, listened to the same music, etc., that those same feelings would be there too. And of course...they never were...because as it turns out, that isn't something any of us can do. Doesn't stop us trying though. You know what? In so many ways, the life I ended up with so far has been so much more epic and satisfying than I expected, too. I never knew just how good it would feel to be really loved by a good man in spite of my flaws. I never knew how strong and loving the bond between mother and child was...I didn't know, either, that my kids would be so cool and that watching them grow up would be so fun. Happiness is not constant but that doesn't mean it's not present. It is! Embrace the good times when they come, because they will come. Enjoy the heck out of them. That's what gets you through the hard times. You can't live forever in happiness but you can live in it sometimes. Your life will, I think, prove to be in many ways better than what you expected even though right now you're sad.

Honestly, a huge part of life has been learning to accept that what's going on isn't what we expected, or that the way we feel isn't living up to our expectations, and learning to shift our expectations and goals accordingly. Nothing is free; every choice we make has a consequence and requires in some way a sacrifice from us. Saying yes to one thing means saying no to another. Saying yes to marrying this man meant also saying yes to being an army wife, which meant saying no to the life you had before. You had to make a sacrifice...you gave up something good that you loved for the sake of building something better. Sacrifice wouldn't be sacrifice if it was easy or painless. Anything good we want to build requires us to sacrifice and work hard. It pays off, but it won't be easy. But I promise you, it will be worth it!

In your case, you are reasonably sad because you left behind a life that you loved and people that you loved...that's hard! Change is rarely easy even when it's a change we welcome. Not only that, but pregnancy hormones can really mess with your emotional state. Be patient. Once you have your baby, your days will be more full than they are right now, and while you will be tired and stressed for the first while (babies are demanding and often inconvenient), you will in time feel more like there is a purpose to being a homemaker. As your family grows and your child (and maybe...children?) grows older, you're going to see the fruit of your hard work, and it will bring you joy. So NO, you will not feel like this forever. It's going to get better in time. If it helps, remind yourself that you are building something worthwhile, and for now, giving up some happiness and personal fulfillment is what you have to do in order to see it through. Give it time. And don't be so hard on yourself; you aren't selfish and ungrateful. You are simply human, feeling normal human things. Life in our society doesn't prepare us for the reality of life; we value instant gratification far too much, and it leaves us feeling adrift when life requires hard things from us. You're not a bad person for feeling this way, or a selfish wife. Nor are you taking anything for granted. You're disappointed. And that's okay.

PS - if,after baby comes, you are still crying every day, please talk to a doctor about getting some help! Depression can be serious, and while yours currently stems from your situation, postpartum depression is physical and can be treated. There's no shame in asking for help. Hang in there, love; it gets better.
